paragraphs.heading: What Gondwana was
paragraphs.text: Gondwana was a large landmass, usually described as a supercontinent. What is left of it makes up around two-thirds of today's continental area: Africa, South America, Antarctica, Australia, the Indian subcontinent, Arabia and Zealandia. In time it was the biggest piece of continental crust of the Paleozoic Era, with an area of some 100,000,000 km², about a fifth of the Earth's surface. By the earliest definition, though, it did not count as a supercontinent, because the landmasses of Baltica, Laurentia and Siberia lay apart from it.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The name is borrowed from a region of India. That region's name comes from Sanskrit and means 'forest of the Gonds'. The Austrian scientist Eduard Suess gave the name to the continent. It had been used in geology before, first by Medlicott in 1872. Some scientists prefer to call the supercontinent "Gondwanaland", so that it is clearly distinguished from the region.

paragraphs.heading: A slow assembly
paragraphs.text: Gondwana took a long time to come together, over the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic. The process is still not fully understood, because paleomagnetic data are lacking. A group of events known together as the Pan-African orogeny brought the continental fragments of a much older supercontinent, Rodinia, together. The pieces did not all arrive at once. Around 600 million years ago most of western Gondwana had already joined up, while Australia and East Antarctica were still apart from India, eastern Africa and Kalahari. India reached its place in Gondwana by about 550 million years ago, and Australia and East Antarctica merged with the rest between about 570 and 530 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: What else was happening
paragraphs.text: While Gondwana's assembly was in its last stages, the Iapetus Ocean was opening between western Gondwana and Laurentia. The Cambrian explosion took place during this interval. For a brief period near the boundary between the Precambrian and the Cambrian, Laurentia lay docked along the western shores of a united Gondwana. Together they formed Pannotia, a short-lived and still disputed supercontinent.

paragraphs.heading: Joining Pangaea, then breaking up
paragraphs.text: During the Carboniferous, Gondwana fused with Laurasia to form Pangaea. In the Triassic it began to separate from Laurasia, the northern part of Pangaea, and in the Early Jurassic, around 180 million years ago, it started to break into fragments. The final stages came in the Paleogene, from around 66 to 23 million years ago, when the Antarctic land bridge broke up. Antarctica separated from South America and Australia, which formed the Drake and Tasmanian Passages. The regions that once belonged to Gondwana shared elements of plant and animal life that persist to the present day.

paragraphs.heading: Pieces that crossed to Asia
paragraphs.text: South-east Asia was put together from Gondwanan and Cathaysian continental fragments. The rifting along Gondwana's northern margin can be divided into three phases. In the first, in the Devonian, North and South China, with Tarim and Quidam in north-western China, rifted and opened the Paleo-Tethys behind them. In the Early Permian, the opening of the Neo-Tethys Ocean along the same margin produced a long series of such fragments, called terranes, which today run from Turkey to north-eastern India. As the Neo-Tethys widened in the Permian and Triassic, it pushed all of these terranes across the Equator and over to Eurasia.
